questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless genital ulcer with a clean base, indurated edges, and a rubbery consistency. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: This is a classic description of primary syphilis (chancre) caused by Treponema pallidum. The painless, indurated ulcer with non-tender lymphadenopathy is characteristic. Haemophilus ducreyi causes painful chancroid; Calymmatobacterium granulomatis causes donovanosis (granuloma inguinale); Chlamydia trachomatis causes lymphogranuloma venereum.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer develops a slowly expanding erythematous plaque with an active scaly border on the trunk. KOH mount shows thick-walled, brown, septate hyphae and round muriform cells. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is caused by dematiaceous (melanized) fungi and shows characteristic 'copper penny' (sclerotic/muriform) bodies on histology and KOH mount. These are thick-walled, dark-brown, septate cells. Tinea corporis would show thin-walled hyphae; sporotrichosis shows cigar-shaped yeast; mycetoma shows grains.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with leprosy on dapsone therapy presents with acute onset hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia, and peripheral neuropathy. The most likely cause is:
questions.exp: Dapsone toxicity causes dose-dependent hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia, which are its most common adverse effects. G6PD deficiency predisposes to severe hemolysis. Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DDS syndrome) is an idiosyncratic reaction typically occurring 4-6 weeks after starting therapy with fever, exfoliative dermatitis, and hepatitis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with a 2-month history of multiple grouped vesicles on erythematous plaques over extensor surfaces and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophilic infiltrate at tips of dermal papillae. The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: This is Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH), characterized by intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces and buttocks. Histology shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae tips. Dapsone gives dramatic symptomatic relief. Gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment. DH is associated with celiac disease and IgA deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:640, speckled pattern). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies are positive. The most specific antibody for this diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibodies are the most specific antibody for SLE (though less sensitive than anti-dsDNA). Anti-dsDNA is highly specific but can fluctuate with disease activity. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjogren's syndrome. Anti-histone antibodies are associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male with a long-standing varicose ulcer develops a raised, indurated, flesh-colored nodule at the ulcer margin. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. This malignant transformation in a chronic ulcer is called:
questions.exp: Marjolin's ulcer is a malignant (usually squamous cell carcinoma) transformation occurring in chronic wounds, scars, or ulcers. It is typically well-differentiated but aggressive due to immune privilege of scar tissue. It does not metastasize early. Bowen's disease is SCC in situ; verrucous carcinoma is a low-grade variant; keratoacanthoma is usually self-resolving.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with hypopigmented anesthetic patches. Slit-skin smear shows no bacilli. Skin biopsy shows non-caseating epithelioid granulomas destroying dermal nerves. Lepromin test is strongly positive. The classification is:
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) shows strong cell-mediated immunity (positive lepromin test), few lesions (1-5), well-defined hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation, absent/sparse bacilli (paucibacillary), and epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytic infiltrate destroying nerve fibers. BT also shows similar features but with less defined immunity and more lesions.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a tense bullae on normal-appearing skin predominantly involving the flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense bullae (often on normal or urticarial skin), linear IgG and C3 deposits at the BMZ on DIF, and antibodies against BP180 and BP230 antigens in the lamina lucida. Pemphigus vulgaris shows flaccid bullae with intraepidermal IgG deposits. DH shows granular IgA at papillary tips. Linear IgA shows linear IgA deposits.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with extensive verrucous plaques on the face and perianal region. Histology shows koilocytes and intranuclear inclusions. The most common HPV type associated with this presentation in HIV patients is:
questions.exp: In immunocompromised patients (HIV, organ transplant recipients), HPV types 5 and 8 (associated with Epidermodysplasia Verruciformis or EV) cause extensive verrucous lesions. These are usually benign in immunocompetent individuals but can become widespread and malignant in immunocompromised hosts. HPV 6 and 11 cause genital warts; HPV 16 causes anogenital malignancy.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, and calcinosis cutis. Esophageal dysmotility is also noted. The most likely positive antibody is:
questions.exp: This is CREST syndrome (Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis), characterized by Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia. Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are positive in ~80% of limited SSc/CREST. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse SSc and ILD. Anti-RNA Pol III correlates with diffuse SSc and renal crisis. Anti-Jo-1 is for dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male presents with multiple discrete, dome-shaped, pearly papules with central umbilication on the trunk and extremities. Giemsa stain of expressed material shows large intracytoplasmic inclusions (Henderson-Paterson bodies). The causative organism belongs to:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscipoxvirus, a member of the Poxviridae family. The characteristic Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies are large intracytoplasmic inclusions seen on Giemsa stain. The lesions are self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals but can be extensive in HIV-positive patients.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a painless nodule on the dorsum of the foot that has been growing slowly for 10 years. Examination shows multiple sinuses discharging white grains. The diagnosis and treatment of choice are:
questions.exp: Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) presents with the triad of painless swelling, sinuses, and grains. White/pale grains suggest Madurella grisea or Pseudallescheria boydii. Treatment requires prolonged antifungal therapy (itraconazole) combined with surgery. Actinomycetoma (bacterial) requires antibiotics like cotrimoxazole and amikacin. The clinical triad is key to diagnosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with perifollicular hemorrhagic papules and corkscrew hairs, particularly on the lower limbs. He has a history of poor nutrition. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency) classically presents with perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew (swan-neck) hairs, and impaired wound healing. Vitamin C is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis. Phrynoderma (Vitamin A deficiency) causes follicular hyperkeratosis with dry, scaly skin. Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica-like picture.

questions.q: During a Mohs micrographic surgery, the surgeon identifies a remaining positive margin. The technique used to examine the removed tissue that makes Mohs unique is:
opts: Horizontal (en face) frozen sections examining 100% of margins
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery uses horizontal (en face) frozen sections that allow examination of 100% of the surgical margins (both peripheral and deep margins simultaneously). This is its key advantage over traditional bread-loaf (vertical) sectioning which samples only a small percentage of the margin. This precision allows highest cure rates with maximum tissue conservation.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male on long-term hydroxyurea for polycythemia vera develops multiple painful ulcers on bilateral malleoli. He also has hyperpigmented, atrophic skin changes. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Discontinue hydroxyurea and switch to anagrelide
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea-induced leg ulcers are a well-recognized complication of long-term hydroxyurea therapy, typically occurring on the malleoli. The only effective treatment is discontinuation of hydroxyurea. Switching to an alternative agent (like anagrelide or ruxolitinib for the underlying condition) is recommended. The ulcers usually heal after stopping the drug.

questions.q: A neonate presents at 2 days of life with diffuse skin blistering, erosions, and positive Nikolsky sign. Skin biopsy shows acantholysis in the granular layer. The causative toxin is produced by which organism?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins (ET-A and ET-B) produced by S. aureus phage group II (especially phage type 71). The toxins cleave desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, causing superficial blistering. In neonates, it presents as Ritter disease. Treatment is IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (oxacillin/cloxacillin).

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with multiple hyperpigmented, scaly plaques with a photosensitive distribution (exposed areas) plus a pellagra-like rash. He has been on isoniazid for tuberculosis. The mechanism of this side effect is:
opts: Inhibition of pyridoxine (B6) metabolism leading to niacin deficiency
questions.exp: Isoniazid (INH) inhibits pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) metabolism by competing with pyridoxal phosphate. Since niacin is synthesized from tryptophan via a B6-dependent pathway, INH therapy can cause pellagra (niacin deficiency) manifesting as dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Treatment includes supplementation with both pyridoxine and niacin.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate develops painful oral ulcers, macrocytosis, and mild hepatotoxicity. The best management is:
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), reducing folate availability. Folic acid supplementation (1-5 mg/day) reduces the incidence of mucositis, oral ulcers, nausea, and hepatotoxicity without compromising efficacy. Leucovorin (folinic acid) is used in high-dose MTX rescue, not for routine supplementation. Methotrexate need not be discontinued unless there is severe toxicity.

questions.q: A 24-year-old female presents with widespread papulopustular acne that worsens premenstrually. She is on oral contraceptive pills. Which progestin-containing OCP would be most beneficial for her acne?
questions.exp: Cyproterone acetate is a potent anti-androgen that blocks androgen receptors, making it beneficial for acne and hirsutism. OCPs containing cyproterone acetate (e.g., Diane-35) are particularly effective for hormonally driven acne. Levonorgestrel and norgestrel have androgenic activity and can worsen acne. Desogestrel has low androgenic activity but is less potent than cyproterone.

questions.q: A 68-year-old male presents with a slow-growing, firm nodule on the nose, present for 3 years. Dermoscopy shows arborizing blood vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests. The treatment with highest cure rate for this tumor is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose is in an H-zone (high-risk area for recurrence). Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (~99% for primary BCC) with maximum tissue conservation. It is indicated for facial BCCs, especially those on the H-zone, recurrent BCCs, morpheaform/infiltrative type, and tumors >2cm. Standard excision has higher recurrence rates in high-risk locations.

questions.q: A 40-year-old presents with symmetrical hyperpigmentation on the malar eminences, forehead, and upper lip, worsened by sun exposure. She is pregnant. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of pigmentation. The most appropriate treatment after delivery is:
questions.exp: Melasma typically involves epidermal pigment (which enhances under Wood's lamp). The modified Kligman's formula – triple combination cream containing hydroquinone (4%), tretinoin (0.05%), and fluocinolone acetonide (0.01%) – is the gold standard first-line treatment post-partum. During pregnancy, only sunscreen and topical azelaic acid are considered safe. Triple combination works synergistically.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with multiple soft, compressible papules and nodules distributed in a dermatomal pattern on the trunk. His father had similar lesions. Histology shows encapsulated masses of Schwann cells and fibroblasts. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Schwannomatosis (NF3) is characterized by multiple schwannomas without vestibular schwannomas (unlike NF2) and without neurofibromas (unlike NF1). Lesions are painful and follow dermatomal distribution. It is associated with mutations in SMARCB1 or LZTR1 genes. NF1 shows neurofibromas and Café-au-lait macules; NF2 shows bilateral vestibular schwannomas; MEN 2b shows mucosal neuromas.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with a solitary, painless, pearly nodule with telangiectatic vessels on his ear helix. He has extensive actinic damage. The most important risk factor for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma versus basal cell carcinoma in this location is:
questions.exp: Chronic ultraviolet radiation (UVA and UVB) exposure is the most important risk factor for both BCC and SCC. UV radiation induces cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers causing characteristic C→T and CC→TT mutations in p53 (SCC) and PTCH1 (BCC). SCC on the ear helix has high risk of metastasis. Other risk factors include radiation, chronic wounds, immunosuppression, and arsenic exposure.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with erythematous, well-demarcated, annular plaques with an active peripheral border on the trunk. KOH examination is negative. Skin biopsy shows palisading granulomas with central mucin deposition. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Granuloma annulare (GA) shows palisading granulomas with central mucin (necrobiosis with mucin) surrounded by histiocytes, lymphocytes, and fibroblasts. The lesions are skin-colored to red annular plaques, KOH negative. Tinea shows fungal hyphae on KOH. Necrobiosis lipoidica shows necrobiosis with lipid and plasma cells, typically on shins. Sarcoidosis shows naked (non-caseating) granulomas without mucin.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with psoriasis presents with a new-onset warm, swollen, deformed right index finger (sausage digit). She has nail pitting and onycholysis. Radiograph shows a 'pencil-in-cup' deformity. This is characteristic of:
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is seronegative (RF negative), and arthritis mutilans is the most severe form, characterized by osteolysis causing 'pencil-in-cup' deformity on X-ray and 'telescoping' digits (opera glass hand). Dactylitis (sausage digit) is a hallmark of PsA. RA is seropositive and causes symmetric polyarthritis. Gout shows urate crystals; reactive arthritis follows infection.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male immigrant presents with a verrucous, cauliflower-like mass on the perianal region. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous epithelium with prominent koilocytes and no frank malignancy. HPV typing reveals HPV 6. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Buschke-Lowenstein tumor (giant condyloma acuminatum) is a locally destructive, large, verrucous tumor associated with HPV 6 and 11 (low-risk types). Histologically it appears benign (well-differentiated squamous epithelium with koilocytes) but behaves aggressively with local invasion. Treatment is wide local excision. Bowenoid papulosis is associated with HPV 16 and shows dysplasia; SCC shows frank malignancy.

questions.q: A 52-year-old male presents with a non-healing ulcer on the hard palate and nose. He has a history of travel to South America. Serology for Leishmania is positive. The treatment of choice for this mucosal form of disease is:
questions.exp: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (espundia), caused by L. braziliensis, affects the mucous membranes (nose, mouth, palate) and is refractory to treatment. Liposomal amphotericin B is preferred for mucosal disease due to its efficacy and safety profile. Miltefosine is an oral option but has teratogenic risk. Intralesional treatment is for cutaneous disease only. Topical paromomycin is for cutaneous leishmaniasis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with SLE develops a widespread, photosensitive, annular erythematous eruption with scaling after starting hydrochlorothiazide. Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies are strongly positive. She is diagnosed with:
questions.exp: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) is strongly associated with anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (>80%). It presents as photosensitive, annular-polycyclic or papulosquamous lesions on sun-exposed areas. SCLE can be triggered or exacerbated by drugs including thiazides, calcium channel blockers, TNF inhibitors, and proton pump inhibitors. DLE presents with discoid scarring plaques; acute CLE presents with malar rash.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male presents with painful swelling of his lower lip, recurrent episodes of facial edema, and fissured tongue. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is characterized by the classic triad of: (1) recurrent orofacial swelling (cheilitis granulomatosa), (2) relapsing facial palsy, and (3) fissured (scrotal/plicated) tongue. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Treatment includes intralesional corticosteroids. Orofacial granulomatosis is the broader term; Crohn's disease can also cause similar biopsy findings but typically has GI involvement.

questions.q: A 55-year-old female presents with progressive tightening of facial skin, perioral wrinkles, and inability to open the mouth fully. She has digital ulcers and pulmonary fibrosis. Antibody testing is most likely to show:
questions.exp: Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) is characterized by extensive skin involvement proximal to the elbows and knees, plus internal organ involvement (pulmonary fibrosis, renal crisis). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is positive in ~30-40% of dcSSc and is associated with pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc/CREST. Anti-RNA Pol III with renal crisis. Anti-Jo-1 with dermatomyositis.
